briefs.headline: 'Making my job easier': Zaheer Khan opens up on Dhoni's 'unexpected' retirement
briefs.deck: Dhoni will no longer take the field for CSK but will remain associated with the five-time champions as their team mentor from IPL 2027. Zaheer said the team would miss having Dhoni as a player but was looking forward to working with him in his new role.
briefs.bodyText:
Chennai Super Kings
 head coach 
Zaheer Khan
 has admitted that MS Dhoni's decision to retire from playing in the 
Indian Premier League
 came as a surprise to him, while describing the end of the former captain's playing career as an emotional moment for the franchise.
Dhoni will no longer take the field for CSK but will remain associated with the five-time champions as their team mentor from IPL 2027. Zaheer said the team would miss having Dhoni as a player but was looking forward to working with him in his new role.
"It's been an emotional week for all of us, with mixed feelings. Every year, you're hoping that MS is going to be seen playing a role for the team this season. He will be, but in a different avatar, and hence the mixed feelings.
"I think the journey he has had in cricket has been amazing. Srinivasan rightly said that there is no CSK without MS, and that surely is the case," Zaheer said in a video uploaded on CSK's YouTube channel.
Dhoni's retirement from playing was confirmed on November 17, when CSK announced that he would take up the role of team mentor.
Zaheer said he was also looking forward to having Dhoni's experience and guidance as he takes charge of the team ahead of the next season.
"It's mixed feelings for me personally because you're not going to see him as part of the playing team. But I'm excited that he's going to be sharing the burden with me, making my job easier, guiding us in the right direction and being a mentor to us.
"So, yeah, excited about that, looking ahead, but also emotional about the decision he has taken," Zaheer added.
Dhoni led CSK to five IPL titles and two Champions League T20 crowns. However, he did not play a single match during the 2026 season because of fitness concerns.
While CSK owner Rupa Gurunath had earlier revealed that Dhoni had indicated he might not return as a player, Zaheer said he had not seriously considered the possibility. His focus, he explained, had been on preparing the squad and planning for the upcoming season.
"Not at all. I think, for a couple of reasons, it was the last year of this cycle. So maybe, looking ahead at a fresh cycle, those kind of thoughts would have popped into my head," Zaheer said.
"But right now, I wasn't even thinking about it. Obviously, you're looking at the season, you're looking at the stack-up of your team, the playing XI. I haven't personally given it a thought because, you know, it's MS. He knows what is the right thing to do and when is the time to act upon a certain thing.
"So I was not really spending my time and energy going in that direction. Whatever it is, it's going to be his decision. I'm planning for the season.
"So, yes, it was unexpected for me personally when he did mention it in a very, very subtle way, as you know, he doesn't like to create massive news out of it. It just was in the discussion, casually mentioning that, okay, this is it, you're going to have some extra money to go into the auction with," Zaheer added.

briefs.headline: 'More stress than fun': Carlsen says his entry at Total Chess Pilot was 'unfortunate'
briefs.deck: "When it's about this tournament I'll say that my entry was unfortunate," he said, as quoted by ChessBase.
briefs.bodyText:
Magnus Carlsen
 has admitted that he was not in the right frame of mind to compete at the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot in Budapest, saying his participation in the tournament had been "unfortunate". The five-time world champion also said he was frustrated with the way people in the chess world questioned his statements.
Carlsen made the comments in an interview with TV2 Norge after winning the second blitz game against Vladislav Artemiev on Thursday. Asked about the controversy surrounding him at the tournament, the Norwegian said, "It annoys me a little, everything that's happening. I can say more generally, what annoys me the absolute most in the chess world is that people do not believe me on what I say. I always speak exactly what I think and exactly how I intend it."
Explaining his concerns about taking part in the event, Carlsen said he had been away from his family for a long time and was not keen to play tournaments unless there was a significant sporting or financial incentive.
"When it's about this tournament I'll say that my entry was unfortunate," he said, as quoted by ChessBase.
"I was not in the state of playing chess right now, because it's a long time to be away from my family right now. 
And it's a point in my career where I necessarily don't want to play tournaments where there's not a lot of stakes, where it's either very important or very lucrative. And here this was more stressful than fun. And of course that's a bad entry to have to a tournament, and then everything gets very amplified when I was not very motivated to begin with," Carlsen said.
Magnus Carlsen's high-stakes gamble pays off
Carlsen took an unusual route to protecting his place at the top of world chess, forfeiting two games against Vladislav Artemiev before producing a must-win performance in the Fast Classic to secure his first victory in the format at the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot in Budapest on Thursday.
The five-time world champion, competing for 17th place, turned a 3-9 deficit into an 11-9 victory, winning the Fast Classic game to complete an extraordinary comeback. The result also lifted his live rating to 2804, keeping him above the coveted 2,800 Elo mark and retaining his world No. 1 status.
After skipping his Fast Classic games against Bibisara Assaubayeva for two consecutive days, Carlsen chose to sit out of the rapid section this time against Vladislav Artemiev.
Carlsen had won three of the four blitz games, but forfeited both rapid games, leaving him needing the eight-point Fast Classic win to take the day.
With the win, Carlsen's live rating also improved to 2804.
Carlsen's rating and ranking were genuinely under threat. A draw against Artemiev in the Fast Classic would have taken his rating down to 2799, marking the first time in 17 years that he would have fallen below 2,800. A defeat, coupled with a win for Fabiano Caruana, would also have opened the door for the American to become world No. 1.

briefs.headline: Akash Deep 2.0 is better, smarter and stronger
briefs.deck: Akash Deep recently returned to Test cricket after a 15-month injury hiatus. He showcased his skills by taking three wickets in his comeback match. Previously, he had faced challenges including a stress fracture during the Ranji Trophy. Akash expressed gratitude for the support from the Indian team management throughout his recovery. His performance highlighted his dedication and hard work…
briefs.bodyText:
Even after receiving the generous acknowledgement of “well bowled” from 
Glenn Phillips
, Akash Deep wasn’t quite ready to celebrate. The New Zealand centurion had just been castled by a beauty, but the Dehri-born Bengal pacer first looked back at umpire Kumar Dharmasena to check whether his front foot had landed all right. Only after getting the nod from the Sri Lankan did Akash allow himself a celebration.
Akash had good reason to look back and check. On his Test debut in Ranchi in Feb 2024, he had sent Zak Crawley’s off-stump cartwheeling, only for his joy to be cut short by the dreaded noball siren after umpire Rod Tucker got the message in his ear-piece from who else, but Dharmasena that Akash had overstepped. For someone who had waited so long for his India cap, after even having to fight with his late father for the right to pursue cricket instead of taking up a job, the wait for a maiden Test wicket was extended by a few more overs.
His career since has followed a similarly stop-start path. One of the heroes of India’s 2-2 series draw in England, highlighted by his 10-wicket haul at Edgbaston in Aug 2025, Akash’s struggle-filled journey of economic hardship, grief and relentless hustle took another turn when he suffered a stress fracture of the back while playing the 
Ranji Trophy
 semifinal against Jammu & Kashmir in Kalyani last Feb.
Just two months earlier, Kolkata Knight Riders had picked him up for Rs 1 crore after Lucknow Super Giants, who had paid Rs 8 cr for him, released him. 
Following surgery and months of rehabilitation at the Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru, Akash was grateful for the trust and support shown by the Indian team management.
On Friday, returning to Test cricket after a 15-month hiatus, he repaid that faith with 3-53 from 23 overs. His previous Test appearance had come against England at the Oval.
“GG sir (head coach 
Gautam Gambhir
) used to follow up during that period and he would keep asking, ‘kaisa chal raha hain?’” Akash said after the day’s play. “During that time, I worked on my bowling and on areas I could improve. I wanted to get stronger. It didn’t feel like I was playing international cricket after nearly one and a half years.”
Perhaps that was because Akash had already put plenty of miles into his legs. He bowled 23.2 overs in the Irani Cup against Rest of India in Srinagar, followed by 33 overs for Bengal against Delhi at Kalyani. He then delivered 35.3 overs in the first India A-New Zealand A game in Lincoln and another 23 in the second in Christchurch.
Apart from rehabilitation at the COE, Akash used his time away to work on his craft. In 11 Tests, Akash has 31 wickets, with 11 of those victims bowled. Harry Brook, Joe Root, Zak Crawley, Ben Duckett and Ollie Pope feature on an impressive list of batters whose defences Akash has breached.
Phillips, though, might rank as the best of the lot. Akash went wide on the crease and angled the ball in. After pitching, it moved away sharply to beat Phillips and rearrange his stumps. It was Bumrahesque, but Akash describes it matter-of-factly.
“The ball wasn’t doing much, so I was trying to move wider of the crease to play with the mind of the batter. I was trying to make the batter play. So I went out. The batter started to play me, whereas he was leaving me earlier. Then I switched again, and got the wicket. I was trying to play with the batters’ mind,” Akash said.

briefs.headline: Cricket's billion-dollar blind spot: The search for a global gaming franchise
briefs.deck: Cricket has millions of fans and a growing gaming audience, but it is yet to produce a video game franchise with global reach. As the ICC explores the commercial potential of its gaming rights, Indian studio LightFury Games believes the opportunity lies in building a cricket title with the depth and ambition of a AAA game. Co-founder Karan Shroff explains the gap, the challenge and India's larger…
briefs.bodyText:
As Grand Theft Auto VI finally arrives, 13 years after its predecessor, the excitement surrounding one of gaming's biggest franchises is a reminder of what a truly enduring video game can mean to its audience. The anticipation has been years in the making, with GTA V continuing to command a massive following even as an entire generation of gaming technology has evolved around it.
Cricket gaming has its own version of that nostalgia, although without quite the same succession of blockbusters. Nearly two decades after its release, EA Sports Cricket 07 continues to find a place in conversations among fans, many of whom still regard it as a benchmark for the genre. There have been attempts to fill that void, from the Don Bradman series to Ashes Cricket and more recent mobile titles, some of which have reached millions of downloads, but cricket is yet to produce a game that can build the kind of sustained global following enjoyed by EA Sports FC or NBA 2K.
The International Cricket Council, too, is now looking at that space more seriously. What began with a global call for expressions of interest in 2025 to develop a flagship mobile cricket game moved into a formal tender process in April this year, with some of the biggest names in gaming, including Electronic Arts, Big Ant Studios and Krafton, alongside Indian companies such as Reliance Jio, Nazara Technologies and Dream Cricket, reported to be among those interested.
 The rights framework being considered by the ICC covers player names, images and likenesses, tournament data and branding across mobile and console platforms, although the process has involved several stages of evaluation and the final arrangement has not been publicly confirmed.
It is a fairly crowded field for a category that has struggled to produce a lasting global franchise. Cricket has had its share of successful titles and loyal players, but the interest has not quite translated into a game that travels beyond the sport's traditional markets, or one that can keep players engaged over several years. The ICC's move has brought the commercial side of that opportunity into focus, but for developers the question is a little more basic: what has been missing from cricket games all these years, and what would it take to get it right?
The cricket gaming industry's missing global franchise
Karan Shroff, co-founder of Bengaluru-based LightFury Games, believes there is still a sizeable gap to be filled. The company is developing eCricket, a mobile-first title that it hopes will go beyond the familiar format of a cricket game and build into a longer-term gaming property. But Shroff's ambition is not restricted to making another cricket game. He wants to build a gaming studio from India that can create intellectual property for a global audience, with eCricket serving as its first major test.
"While eCricket is our first product and it's the first game that we'll build as a startup, all our energy and focus is on that. But we are not a one-game, one-product company. So LightFury is a AAA studio and a game tech company and that's the vision that we're building on," Shroff tells Timesofindia.com.
"Imagine if, I mean you look at China, they have Tencent, they have NetEase, you look at the US, they have EA, they have Rockstar, you look at France, they have Ubisoft and so on and so forth. But what does India have from a gaming company? Not too much, unfortunately. And that's something that we want to change worldwide. We want to build AAA IPs from India that go global."
Building more than just another cricket game
The choice of cricket came from looking at a category where there was already an audience, but where he felt the larger opportunity had not been explored.
"When we got together we were like, okay, what space has a white space broadly where there hasn't been a AAA product but there is a market to capture. And cricket was of course there. There were a lot of mid-core, casual games that are doing well, but not a AAA title," he said.
"When you look at that market, they have 100, 200 million downloads but poor retention. And that's something we wanted to bridge. High-quality products, you know, AAA products are built with all the bells and whistles, be it the progression, the task system, the meta system, the monetisation and how you go about the journey within a game, the storytelling, the fidelity, all of those things matter a lot when you build a AAA title. And it's a long journey, it takes years to get there."
The history of cricket games is not short. Titles such as Graham Gooch's Test Cricket, Brian Lara Cricket and the EA Sports Cricket series appeared across successive generations of consoles and computers. Cricket 07, released in November 2006, became the last EA Sports cricket game for home consoles and PC. Codemasters' Brian Lara series also had a following, with its 2005 release reaching the top of the UK all-formats sales chart.
The genre did not stop there. Big Ant Studios developed the Don Bradman Cricket series before moving to Ashes Cricket and the Cricket titles that followed. Its latest release, Cricket 26, includes an expanded Ashes mode, a management career mode and a Pro Team format with multiplayer competition. Mobile developers have also built their own audiences through titles such as Real Cricket.
The continued presence of these games points to an audience, but the challenge has been keeping players engaged and finding a following beyond cricket's established markets. Shroff believes two areas in particular have held cricket games back: licensing and the way the sport is recreated in the game.
"One is of course the licensing. So, you know, we misspell the names. We don't have accurate licences for things. I think that's a very important aspect of what we do. So we've gone ahead and closed about 600 cricketers overall, and everybody from Rohit to Dhoni to Jos Buttler to Joe Root, we have all of these guys and many more," he said.
"Every player in our game is a real-world athlete. So no fake names, you know, and they look like themselves, they play like themselves."
LightFury has secured licences for more than 600 cricketers through its partnership with Winners Alliance, with players from several major cricketing nations included in the roster. For Shroff, licensing is not simply about getting the names and faces of popular cricketers into the game. It is also about making sure their abilities are reflected in how they play.
"You can't build a AAA title and not have the right athlete. It shows the seriousness behind the vision and the thought process, which is very clear from day one, that every athlete in the game will be a real-world athlete. Not just from a look and likeness perspective but even from the way they play in game," he said.
"So, for example, can you bowl and bat with an MSD? No. And can you wicket-keep with a Hardik Pandya? No. You can place him as a wicketkeeper but he'll be an awful wicketkeeper. On the other hand, you bowl with an MSD, he won't be a good bowler. That needs to apply overall from a gameplay perspective as well. You take Hardik Pandya, one of the best all-rounders in the world, you should have that experience and leverage in gameplay."
The licensing and gameplay challenge
The licensing effort also feeds into the game's Ultimate Squad format, where players can build a team by bringing together cricketers from different countries and eras. Rather than being restricted to an existing international or domestic side, users can assemble a squad around the players they want, with individual attributes intended to influence how they perform in the game.
"The way we are building our team is on the back of the Ultimate Squad. So you will have your progression where you complete tasks and move forward. But you will also have the opportunity, as you complete tasks, to get rewards and then go and unlock better cards and build your Ultimate Squad and then take that online and compete with other players. If you beat them again, you get better rewards and you're able to build a better team," Shroff said.
"So you're kind of chasing your ultimate squad broadly. Like can I have hypothetically Rohit, Dhoni, Bumrah, Pandya, Jos Buttler, Joe Root, all of these guys in one team? And Bumrah opening the bowling attack, can I have it? I can, but I need to play and make that progression and build my ultimate squad."
LightFury plans to launch with multiplayer and Ultimate Squad, while a career mode and other features are expected to be introduced later. Shroff said the company has mapped out more than three years of development and content, with new features to be added as players become familiar with the game.
"All of the other features that you're talking about, in terms of can I start my journey in cricket and go all the way through, when a match is being played can I have a play-along moment, all of that is something that we'll build in the future. But as of now when we go live, it's a AAA title so we won't have all the features when we ship. It's a live-services game, we'll keep adding it incrementally," he said.
Building an ecosystem around the game
There is also a commercial calculation behind that approach as LightFury intends to follow a freemium model, with in-app purchases as its primary source of revenue. Players will be able to buy in-game currency, player packs and other items, while those who do not want to spend money can earn currency through reward-based advertising. The company says it does not intend to interrupt matches with advertisements, with ads restricted to reward-based options in the near future.
"I think it's always IAPs (In-App Purchases), as a business, as a game. And if you look at any of the success worldwide, they are a very thriving economy within the game. And they're driven by IAPs. They're not driven by ads. And that's what we want to do as well. We want to thrive on IAPs," Shroff said.
"Of course we will have ads. So it's a freemium kind of a model. So you can either buy currency in game or you can buy a player pack, which is randomized and you end up landing a player and you go about building your ultimate squad. Or you could watch several ads and collect some currency and still go ahead and buy that."
He said the company was conscious of the experience during matches. "One thing that we are very conscious of is user experience. So you will not see ads in game when you're playing, at least for the near future. We're never going to do that. But you will see ads only reward-based."
The scale of the Indian gaming market gives developers a substantial audience to work with, although the numbers need to be read in the context of how different reports define a gamer. The FICCI-EY Media and Entertainment Report 2026 estimated that India's gamer base reached between 515 million and 525 million in 2025, with more than 100 million people playing games daily.
A separate Dentsu-IWMBuzz India Gaming Report 2026 estimated 535 million past-year pure-play gamers, including 332 million who had played in the previous three months and 109 million current paying gamers. It valued the pure-play gaming market at Rs 14,344 crore in 2026. The two sets of figures use different definitions and measurement periods, but underline the scale of the audience that India's gaming industry can potentially reach.
India's gaming opportunity and the global ambition
The bigger challenge is turning that audience into successful home-grown intellectual property that can compete internationally. Shroff wants eCricket to find players in countries where cricket does not have the cultural presence it enjoys in India, England or Australia. He believes gaming can introduce people to the sport before they begin following it.
"100%. 100%. I'll tell you why. The next generation of audience isn't going to be passive. They're not going to just sit and watch. They're going to be immersed in the sport. They're going to want to be a part of it in some fashion and manner," he said.
"Our generation, we all had a say on what the team should be, who should open, why is he bowling, and they shouldn't have got him now, they should have given it to this bowler. This was our social layer on the game which we would have conversations around. We're all passionate about the sport. Similarly, the coming generation is more immersed in the sport. They want to actually be involved in that."
He pointed to the way audiences now engage with sports through content and gaming, rather than only watching matches.
"It's also easy to pick and play. Downloading a game is easy and you learn the ropes while you play the game. It's fun and engaging versus actually taking the sport and going there. The game reaches faster than the sport in a lot of geographies and then eventually the sport reaches there if the game has good penetration," he said.
He drew comparisons with football, WWE and poker, where gaming has helped people become familiar with sports or formats they may not otherwise have followed. For cricket, the possibility is relevant in markets such as the United States, Germany and Japan, where the sport has a smaller following than in India, England or Australia.
The competition for players' time and spending is considerable. Electronic Arts reported net revenue of $7.53 billion for the financial year ended March 2026, with its global football franchise among the major contributors. Its filings also underline the importance of live services and additional in-game content to the business. Building a successful sports game is not just about selling a title; it is about maintaining a player base and a commercial relationship over several years.
Cricketers back LightFury's global ambitions
LightFury has also brought several prominent cricketers into the company as investors. MS Dhoni, Jasprit Bumrah, Hardik Pandya, Shreyas Iyer, Ravindra Jadeja, Tilak Varma and Sai Sudharsan have backed the studio, with Rohit Sharma subsequently joining the group. Their involvement brings visibility and a direct connection with the sport, but Shroff was careful not to suggest that the cricketers are involved in the day-to-day development of the title.
"They don't have too much time to give us. Like most investors, the founders have to do the building. Investors come in with support when you need it. But we have to do all the heavyweight lifting," he said.
He added that some players have asked to receive new builds of the game so they can play them and offer feedback. LightFury also works with Ranji and former IPL cricketers on aspects of the product, while the company looks to use the experience of current players to understand what feels right and what needs to change.
The studio has said it has received more than 300,000 early-access sign-ups. Shroff said the response on social media and YouTube has been encouraging, with gamers also getting an opportunity to play-test the title ahead of its wider release. But he was clear that early registrations and attention are not the ultimate measure of success for the company.
"The vision from day one is to build the best cricket game in the world and be a global franchise built from India for the world. I can give you numbers saying this is what it would mean, this is what profitability would mean. But I think for us, the biggest win is when the gamers, when India loves the game to begin with, because that's where we're going live first. And then gamers across the world love the cricket game," he said.
"Everybody has said cricket has missed what it should have had. So the day they say, now eCricket is that game, it's a win for us because everything else is a subset. Everything else follows. Once you have the consumer's love and you have their validation, I think that's the validation I would always be hungry for."
Can eCricket become India's first global cricket gaming franchise?
For Shroff, the opportunity is bigger than one title. He sees a cricket gaming property creating work for developers, gaming influencers, creators and people involved in tournaments and sponsorships, with the game eventually becoming the centre of a wider digital cricket ecosystem.
"If you ask me where we would be in 2030, we would have created thousands of jobs, we would have created an ecosystem on the back of this, that would be digitally, I mean cricket digitally would transform on the back of this and also it would be the first billion-dollar title from India and also the first billion-dollar IP for cricket," he said.
"You look at other sports and you look at what those sports have done broadly from a gaming IP perspective, they make billions of dollars in revenue, they touch hearts of millions and millions of fans worldwide. It also builds an economy for the ecosystem. You could have gaming influencers emerge from this tomorrow that would make millions of dollars on the back of being the best gamer. So it creates thousands of jobs and a lot of potential and opportunity for a lot of people."
Shroff said LightFury has repeatedly encountered scepticism when it has spoken about building a AAA cricket game in India. The response, he said, has often been that the country already has several cricket games and none has managed to become a global franchise.
"When we would go and tell people we're building AAA titles, and cricket, they'd be like, AAA, really? India, and cricket, there are a dozen cricket games. How does it make you different? Same questions and the same thing, it can never become a global franchise. We've always believed it will. We truly know it will. And it's just about a lot of hard work and discipline and process that goes into building a AAA title," he said.
"The way India recognises and understands cricket, nobody in the world does. And we know the sport, we live it, breathe it, we watch every single game. Even if other countries are playing, we are sitting and watching it. That's how much we love the game. My point being, we know the game, we just need to know how to build it. And once we get it right, then it's a multi-billion-dollar opportunity."
He does not dismiss the scepticism.
"These people are not wrong because we haven't done it right. So I think once we do is when things change. So if you ask me, can eCricket be that IP, I'd say 101%, but only time will tell if my words are true or not," he said.
"But we have all the ingredients and we're not building for something small. I can tell you one thing confidently. If we fail, we'll fail big, but we won't aim small. We won't build something that is mediocre."
The company is yet to establish whether eCricket can hold an audience at the scale Shroff envisages. The early sign-ups, the licensed roster and the backing of prominent cricketers have given it a start, but the game will have to find players well beyond its initial audience.
"We have big dreams but we know till we make it, we've not made it. So we're going to work that hard to make sure that exactly what you said, cricket should have a global franchise. That's been the dream from day one and that's what we want to achieve with eCricket."

briefs.headline: ILT20 Season 5 preview: Focus on South Africans, Associates as league avoids SA20 clash
briefs.deck: The ILT20’s revised schedule has opened the door for several South African stars to feature without clashing with SA20, while mandatory UAE, Afghanistan and Associate player representation strengthens opportunities for emerging talent. Season 5 of UAE's T20 competition has introduced new playing regulations, including a batter zone to redefine wides and a 60-second shot clock for batting teams.
briefs.bodyText:
Dubai: Faf du Plessis
, 
David Miller
, Tabraiz Shamsi, Heinrich Klaasen, Lizaad Williams and George Linde must have heaved a collective sigh of relief when the ILT20 calendar was announced. They might not have been the only ones. With the UAE-based T20 competition starting on November 21 this time -- avoiding an annual clash with South Africa's SA20 in the process -- the South Africans could play in both the competitions.
Having played the first three seasons in January-February before moving to December-January last time around, the ILT20 has rescheduled the calendar even further this time. With the tournament now due to play its final on December 20, it will allow the likes of Du Plessis, Miller, Klaasen, Williams and Linde to make their debuts in the UAE.
Not just the Proteas. Other players, such as Afghanistan's Rashid Khan, who would otherwise play portion of the ILT20 before jetting off to South Africa, can now play both in their entireties. SA20 Season 5 begins on January 17, 2027.
"My schedule opened up nicely to have this league open for me. It's always been a goal to come play in the UAE. I'm really looking forward to this competition. It's a strong competition. You just can't walk in here and think you're going to score runs and perform. 
You really need to be at your best. So that's also the biggest reason why I came to come play this league," said Gulf Giants captain Klaasen.
Teammate and fellow South African Miller is equally pleased. "With the schedule for the year, with all the different leagues and international (cricket) and so on, I think it does become quite difficult to schedule these sort of tournaments. I am here, this time, because it's not overlapping with SA20. So I think it's a really good thing. It helps me to be here, so I'm really happy," added Miller.
We as South Africans, we analyse the game quite well. We read the game quite well. So I think one of our strong qualities is we're good thinking brains.
Faf du Plessis
Over the last five years, the likes of Du Plessis, Quinton de Kock, Klaasen, Reeza Hendricks, Miller and Rilee Rossouw have set the T20 stage on fire, much like the players from the Caribbean did at one point.
In tournaments involving more than five teams, Du Plessis has produced 5937 runs in this period; De Kock has blasted 5213 runs, Klaasen has 5066 runs and Hendricks is on 3386 runs. With 300 sixes, Klaasen has also brought the crowd to their feet. As have Du Plessis (273), Dewald Brevis (242) and Rossouw (239).
"West Indian cricketers have been blessed with the genuine skills, the natural ability to go after the bowling and they displayed. That's why guys like Chris Gayle and all those guys started playing T20 around the world. So I think for us playing alongside these guys, you get to see what they do as well. We as South Africans, we analyse the game quite well. We read the game quite well. So I think one of our strong qualities is we're good thinking brains. That, with power of playing together and that's a good combination," explained Du Plessis on the eve of the competition.
Heinrich Klaasen during a nets session for the Gulf Giants. (Instagram)
The focus, when Desert Vipers play the MI Emirates in the opener, will not just be on the Proteas. With each squad laden with at least four UAE players, four Afghanistan players, one Ireland player, one player each from Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, plus another from an ICC Associate Member country, it will be a massive learning curve for many.
And that will not just be about occupying the dugout. Every playing XI must include at least two UAE players, two Afghanistan players and one Associate player. That last spot can even go to a third UAE player.
And the UAE players were in demand at the auction. Muhammad Waseem commanded $210,000 from the MI Emirates. U-19 player Alishan Sharafu had Abu Dhabi Knight Riders shelling out $110,000. Aayan Khan and Muhammad Rohid pocketed $95,000 from Dubai Capitals and ADKR, respectively. USA's Amshi De Silva went to ADKR for $100,000.
Colin Munro, David Payne, Faf du Plessis, Heinrich Klaasen, Rashid Khan and Sikandar Raza on the eve of ILT20 Season 5 in Dubai. (ILT20)
"I think it's a great thing that the Associates has been included as a must-play member as well, because I honestly believe that there's a lot of Associate cricketers that are good enough to play in these leagues, but unfortunately, get overlooked. So it's nice to have Associate players.
Sharjah Warriorz's Sikandar Raza finds it to be a useful rule that will allow the Associates to get some exposure and portray their talents.
"So I think it's going to be a very nice mixture of some unknowns mixed with the knowns. But for me, the most important thing would be who has the skillset to be going at one time looking at the data and matchups," he continued.
QUICK SINGLES
Colin Munro, David Payne, Faf du Plessis, Heinrich Klaasen, Rashid Khan and Sikandar Raza on the eve of ILT20 Season 5 in Dubai. (ILT20)
🔴Defending champions Desert Vipers boast of Babar Azam, Naseem Shah, Fakhar Zaman, Shadab Khan and Shimron Hetmyer.
🔴MI Emirates have Rashid Khan, Nicholas Pooran, Fazalhaq Farooqi and Romario Shepherd.
🔴Heinrich Klaasen, David Miller and Liam Livingstone represent the Gulf Giants.
🔴Dubai Capitals squad includes Faf du Plessis, Phil Salt, Marcus Stoinis and Mustafizur Rahman.
🔴Finn Allen, Sunil Narine, Moeen Ali and Jason Holder will play for the Abu Dhabi Knight Riders.
🔴Sharjah Warriorz have James Vince, Sikandar Raza, Mohammad Nabi and Adil Rashid in their midst.
WILDCARDS
🔴After the retentions and auction, teams were allowed to name their wildcards. And some heavyweights of T20 cricket will play the ILT20 Season 5.
🔴ADKR have Andre Russell. Kieron Pollard will turn up for the MI Emirates for a fifth straight season. Tim Seifert is back with the Sharjah Warriorz. Sam Billings is in the Dubai Capitals camp. Akeal Hosein will be with the Gulf Giants while Tom Curran is at the Desert Vipers.
NEW RULESBatter zone:
 ILT20 has introduced a "batter zone" at the popping crease. If the entire ball passes outside this designated area, it will be considered a wide, even if the batter has stepped across the stumps. The existing off-side wide lines and rules still apply to reverse sweeps and switch hits.
Shot clock:
 Earlier, the shot clock applied only to the bowling team; now it will apply to the batting team as well. The batters must be ready for the next over within 60 seconds of the previous one ending. Two warnings will be given per innings. After that, each breach will cost five penalty runs. There are exemptions, however, for injuries, reviews, weather delays and strategic timeouts.

briefs.headline: IND vs NZ, 1st Test: Rahul's departure fails to slow Gill as Pant joins the charge
briefs.bodyText:
Nathan Smith to Rishabh Pant, 1 run.
Nathan Smith to Shubman Gill, On a length and around off, Shubman Gill opens the bat face and guides it through point for a single.
Nathan Smith to Shubman Gill, Good length and on off, Shubman Gill gets behind the line of it and blocks it out.
Tap to make your prediction
Glenn Phillips to Rishabh Pant, Slows it up, full and on leg, Rishabh Pant turns it to short mid-wicket.
Glenn Phillips to Rishabh Pant, Drops it short, around off, Rishabh Pant reaches out and punches it to short cover.
Glenn Phillips to Shubman Gill, Flighted, full and on middle, Shubman Gill eases it down to long on for a run.
Glenn Phillips to Shubman Gill, FOUR! Nicely done! Flatter, full and down the leg side. Shubman Gill gets his front foot out, twists his body and paddles it away to the fine leg fence for a boundary.
Glenn Phillips to Shubman Gill, Floated, full and around leg, Shubman Gill clips it to square leg.
Glenn Phillips to Rishabh Pant, Tossed up, full and on off, Rishabh Pant uses his feet and drills it to long off for a single.
DRINKS! India are well in control of this Test, leading by 34 runs and will look to make it bigger and bigger. Shubman Gill has been excellent with the bat, but he did survive a close LBW shout in the previous over. Rishabh Pant has looked a bit fidgety, and the Kiwis will look to put pressure on him, trying to force a mistake. New Zealand are toiling hard, but things are just not going their way, and this game is slowly getting away from them.
Nathan Smith to Shubman Gill, Pitched up wider of the crease, nipping it back in. Gill gets forward and blocks it to short cover.
Nathan Smith to Shubman Gill, Good length, straighter in line and attacking the stumps. Gill keeps it out.
Nathan Smith to Shubman Gill, FOUR! Rotten luck for Nathan Smith, and the 400 is up for India as well. Pitched full and outside off, shaping it away a wee bit. Gill is drawn into the drive and gets a genuine outside edge that runs away into the vacant deep third fence.
Nathan Smith to Shubman Gill, Just short of a good length, tight line around off stump. Gill presses back and keeps it out.
Nathan Smith to Shubman Gill, India overturn an LBW call. A huge shout for LBW, and it's been given. Shubman Gill has a chat with Rishabh Pant, who gives him a fist bump, and this is reviewed. This is bowled on a nagging length again by Nathan Smith, a bit fuller and around off, angling it back in. Gill leans across to the off side and gets forward to block but is beaten past the inside edge and hit on the flap of the front pad. The third umpire is called in, and initial replays suggest there might be an inside edge. Sonic later confirms the spike, and the third umpire is satisfied with it after checking a lot of different angles, overturning the on-field call. NOT OUT! The interesting thing is that Gill didn't look like he felt that inside edge and the bowler doesn't seem happy with the decision of the third umpire. This could be a massive moment in the game.
Nathan Smith to Shubman Gill, Pitched full of a good length, and angled back in from the fifth-stump line. Gill gets his front leg across and blocks it off.
Jacob Duffy to Shubman Gill, Another attempted bumper, over middle and leg, and this is pulled down to fine leg for a single. India now lead by 30 runs.
Jacob Duffy to Shubman Gill, Dug in well short, slanting it across the off stump. Gill drops his hands down and lets it pass.
Jacob Duffy to Rishabh Pant, No ball! Short ball on leg, stylishly pulled down to fine leg for a single, Jacob Duffy has overstepped here and a No Ball is called.
Jacob Duffy to Shubman Gill, The initial call was for two runs, but in the end, Gill picks up three runs. Full-pitched delivery on off, angling it away. Gill clips it away through mid on and Pant realizes that there's an extra run on offer and pushes his skipper. Matt Henry at wide long on, has to circle around a bit and can't prevent the extra runs.
Jacob Duffy to Rishabh Pant, Dug in short and over leg stump, Pant plays a half pull off the hips and hits it uppishly through the vacant square leg region, picking up a single as well.
Jacob Duffy to Shubman Gill, Short ball again, over middle and leg, and Gill swats the pull off the back foot to deep square leg and turns the strike over.
Jacob Duffy to Shubman Gill, A bumper, just down leg and this one really flies through off the deck. Gill moves out of the way and Tom Blundell has to leap up to colleft it.
Nathan Smith to Rishabh Pant, On a fuller length, darting it back in towards off and middle. Pant blocks it on the front foot.
Nathan Smith to Shubman Gill, Fuller and straighter, Gill uses the angle well and clips it wide of mid on for a single. Gill looks for the second run, but won't get it.
Nathan Smith to Shubman Gill, Good length on off, pushed with gentle hands in front of point.
Nathan Smith to Shubman Gill, A subtle change in angle as Smith goes wider on the crease and lands it around off. The ball jas back in but Gill stays solid in defence.
Nathan Smith to Shubman Gill, Nice and full, attacking off and middle, Gill gets well forward and keeps it out.
Nathan Smith to Shubman Gill, Pitched up outside off, Gill leans on and drives it out to cover.
Jacob Duffy to Rishabh Pant, A really well-directed bumper by Duffy, over middle and leg, and coming in at an awkward height. Pant leans back to pull but the ball sails over his blade and takes something on its way to the keeper. Is there a glove on it? The Kiwis look excited, but their appeal is turned down by the umpire. Rishabh Pant is shaking his head, indicating there's nothing on it, but Tom Latham takes the review. Initial replays suggest that it is straight off the shoulder, and Sonic confirms the same. It stays Not Out and New Zealand have only one review remaining now.
Jacob Duffy to Shubman Gill, Short ball over middle and leg, Gill pulls it off the hips and down to fine leg for a single.
Jacob Duffy to Rishabh Pant, Pant gets off the mark. Shorter and around off, Pant hops up and nurdles it down in front of point for a quick single. A bit of coming together between Gill and Duffy, and there's some words exchanged as well.
Jacob Duffy to Rishabh Pant, Pant will keep throwing caution to the wind, and that's the way he plays. Hard length over middle and leg, Pant comes down the track, backs away and has a swipe across the line, but misses.
Jacob Duffy to Rishabh Pant, Top delivery to the new batter. Sharp bumper, right at the batter, looking to aim it at the badge on the helmet. Rishabh Pant takes evasive action and almost falls over to the off side as he ducks under it.
Jacob Duffy to Shubman Gill, Shortish length on leg, Gill hops up and tucks it off his hips down o deep backward square leg for a single.
Nathan Smith to Rishabh Pant, Fuller in length, outside off. Pant leans on with his hands, with no foot movement, and smothers it to extra cover. End of a succseful over for Nathan Smith.
Nathan Smith to Rishabh Pant, Smith sees Pant coming down the pitch and shortens the length a bit, catching Pant by surprise, who ends up getting hit on the gloves.
Nathan Smith to Rishabh Pant, Just back of a length, in and around off stump. Rishabh Pant is caught on the crease and tentatively keeps it out.
The centurion goes. Rishabh Pant is the next man in.
Nathan Smith to KL Rahul, OUT! CHOPPED ON! There's the breakthrough, and Nathan Smith's perseverance has finally paid off. Smith pitches the ball up around off, gets it to skid through with the angle. KL Rahul looks to wait back and play it with an angled bat through gully, but the ball takes a faint inside edge and goes back onto the stumps. Rahul departs after a sensational knock, and raises his bat to the warm applause of the crowd. India are now 386/3, leading by 18 runs.
Nathan Smith to KL Rahul, Pitched up wide of the off stump, angling back in. Rahul leans across and blocks it to extra cover.
Nathan Smith to Shubman Gill, Back of a length, angled into the hips and worked away behind square leg for a single.
Jacob Duffy to KL Rahul, SIX! Wow, that's been smashed over the ropes. Duffy comes over the wicket now and digs it in a bit short and wide outside off. KL Rahul hops across to the leg side, and thwacks it away over deep cover-point for a biggie.
Jacob Duffy to Shubman Gill, Shorter and around the hips, this is pulled away to deep square leg for a single.
Jacob Duffy to Shubman Gill, Short-pitched delivery over middle, flies through off the deck, an Gill ducks under it with ease.
Jacob Duffy to KL Rahul, An angular bouncer, bashed into the deck and slanted across the right-hander. Rahul sets up to pull but this one skids on more than bouncing up and thuds into the right midriff. The ball rolls down to deep third and a leg bye is taken.
Jacob Duffy to KL Rahul, A bit shorter, over middle and leg, Rahul hops up and tucks it down to square leg.
Jacob Duffy to KL Rahul, Short-pitched delivery around the leg stump, flying through off the deck. Rahul moves inside the line and the ball sails through to the keeper.
Nathan Smith to Shubman Gill, Good length on off, blocked off by Gill.
Nathan Smith to Shubman Gill, A cry of anguish from Gill as he fails to find the gap here. Full and outside off, driven sweetly and to the left of short cover, where the fielder makes a fine stop.

briefs.headline: Squash: Velavan looks to end the year on a high
briefs.bodyText:
At the start of this year, Velavan Senthilkumar wasn’t sure where his squash career was heading. Cut to Thursday night in Doha and he was lifting his third PSA Copper-level trophy of 2026.
Trailing top seed Dimitri Steinmann of Switzerland in the QSF 3 final, Velavan fought back to win 3-2. Prior to this triumph, the 28-year-old from Tamil Nadu won two bronze medals at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games.
“At the start of the year, it was really hard for me,” he told The Hindu. “There was a point where I lost my way. It wasn’t even about the results, I was not able to perform to my potential.”
The road to revival began when Velavan travelled to Prague every six weeks to work with former world No. 1 and French coach Gregory Gaultier, who has been guiding him throughout.
“Technically, I was working on a lot of things, like trying to be a bit more sharp and fluid with my movement... working on good line hitting. I think that’s helped a lot,” said Velavan.
It is to be noted that he also hones his skills under other coaches, including Cyrus Poncha, former India No. 1 Saurav Ghosal and Harinder Pal Singh.
Not over yet
The year is not over for the World No. 38 yet.
The World Squash Team Championships, in Korea from December 15 to 19, is his next big event, and performing well there is his immediate goal.
“First up is a tournament in Hong Kong (HKFC Milwaukee Open) but I’m not sure if I’m going because I still haven’t got my visa. And then, of course, to do well in the team Worlds and hopefully break into the top 20.” Velavan has found his way back again. The task now is to keep moving on it.

briefs.headline: Not a fan of the Ballon d’Or, but Kane deserves it: Schmelzer
briefs.deck: The former Borussia Dortmund full-back talks about learning under Klopp, defending against Robben and training with a young Haaland. He also explains why he believes teams, and not individuals, should win awards
briefs.bodyText:
Marcel Schmelzer played only 16 games for Germany, but for over a decade he was one of the most difficult defenders to get past in the Bundesliga. A product of Borussia Dortmund’s youth academy, he played for the club all his life. He retired from the game four years ago and was a part of the coaching staff at Dortmund. Excerpts from an exclusive interview Schmelzer, who was recently in Kochi to train young players and coaches, gave The Hindu:
This is your first visit to India. The Bundesliga is popular here. Did you have some idea of football in India before coming here?
We have a lot of fans here, I know. To be honest, the first time I heard about Indian football was when they bought so many good players at the end of their career, like Alessandro Del Piero. That was some 10-15 years ago?
Yes, in 2014, for the ISL.
And a former teammate of mine was also in India — Manuel Friedrich. He was living here for sure, but I am not sure whom he played for…
